claim: AAV-GFP infection in spinal cord neurons was highly efficient with an infection rate of 87.4 ± 6.34%.
source: We found that AAV-GFP infection in spinal cord neurons was highly efficient (infection rate: 87.4 ± 6.34%; Figure 1A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing infection rates measured in cultured spinal cord neurons, as shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: AAV-NT-3 infection significantly enhanced NT-3 expression compared to AAV-GFP controls (t = 9.967, df = 15, p<0.0001).
source: AAV-NT-3 infection significantly enhanced NT-3 expression (Figure 1E, t = 9.967, df = 15, p<0.0001) and neurite length of spinal cord neurons (Figure 1F, t = 4.273, df = 73, p<0.0001), as compared to the AAV-GFP controls.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data comparing NT-3 expression between AAV-NT-3 and AAV-GFP treated neurons.

claim: AAV-NT-3 infection significantly enhanced neurite length of spinal cord neurons compared to AAV-GFP controls (t = 4.273, df = 73, p<0.0001).
source: AAV-NT-3 infection significantly enhanced NT-3 expression (Figure 1E, t = 9.967, df = 15, p<0.0001) and neurite length of spinal cord neurons (Figure 1F, t = 4.273, df = 73, p<0.0001), as compared to the AAV-GFP controls.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data measuring neurite length in cultured neurons.

claim: Cells receiving AAV-NT-3 demonstrated a significant increase in NT-3 protein expression compared to PBS and AAV-GFP groups at 5 days and 9 days in culture (F2, 6 = 104.4, F2, 6 = 42.17, p<0.001).
source: However, cells receiving AAV-NT-3 demonstrated a significant increase in NT-3 protein expression as compared to the PBS and AAV-GFP groups at 5 days and 9 days in culture (Fig. 1G, F2, 6 = 104.4, F2, 6 = 42.17, p<0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA assay data measuring NT-3 protein levels in conditioned medium from cultured neurons.

claim: AAV-NT-3 dramatically promoted increases in neurite length, neurite branch points, neurite length/cell body, and neurite branch/cell body of spinal cord neurons.
source: AAV-NT-3 dramatically promoted increases in neurite length (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), neurite branch points (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), neurite length/cell body (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E), and neurite branch/cell body of spinal cord neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data showing morphological changes in cultured neurons over time.

claim: Lysolecithin-induced transient demyelination facilitated the infection of motoneurons and dorsal root ganglion (DRG) neurons following adenovirus injections into the sciatic nerve.
source: We previously demonstrated that lysolecithin-induced transient demyelination facilitated the infection of motoneurons and dorsal root ganglion (DRG) neurons following adenovirus injections into the sciatic nerve (Zhang et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study by Zhang et al., 2010.

claim: Demyelination extended approximately 8.42 ± 2.22 mm proximodistally centered at the injection site.
source: P0 (a marker for peripheral myelin) staining showed that demyelination extended approximately 8.42 ± 2.22 mm proximodistally centered at the injection site (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical staining data measuring the extent of demyelination in sciatic nerves.

claim: Lysolecithin treatment significantly increased GFP expression (five-fold, t = 5.826, df = 8, p<0.0001) compared to the non-treated control group.
source: Compared to the non-treated control group, the lysolecithin treatment significantly increased GFP expression (five-fold, t = 5.826, df = 8, p<0.0001; Figure 2—figure supplement 1D) and decreased P0 expression (6-fold, t = 6.324, df = 8, p<0.0001, Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of immunofluorescence data comparing GFP expression between lysolecithin-treated and control groups.

claim: Lysolecithin treatment significantly decreased P0 expression (6-fold, t = 6.324, df = 8, p<0.0001) compared to the non-treated control group.
source: Compared to the non-treated control group, the lysolecithin treatment significantly increased GFP expression (five-fold, t = 5.826, df = 8, p<0.0001; Figure 2—figure supplement 1D) and decreased P0 expression (6-fold, t = 6.324, df = 8, p<0.0001, Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of immunofluorescence data measuring myelin protein P0 expression.

claim: Axons identified by neurofilament 200 (NF200) immunoreactivity remained intact and were not affected by lysolecithin-induced demyelination (t = 1.065, df = 8, ns).
source: However, axons, identified by neurofilament 200 (NF200) immunoreactivity (IR), remained intact and were not affected by lysolecithin-induced demyelination (t = 1.065, df = 8, ns, compared to the PBS-injected control, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,I).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of immunohistochemical data showing no significant difference in axon density between treated and control groups.

claim: Five weeks after viral vector injection, no significant differences in P0 expression were found between lysolecithin injected and non-injected groups (t = 0.711, df = 8, ns).
source: Five weeks after viral vector injection, no significant differences in P0 expression were found between lysolecithin injected and non-injected groups (t = 0.711, df = 8, ns, Figure 2—figure supplement 1F,J).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of immunofluorescence data showing remyelination at 5 weeks post-injection.

claim: In the lysolecithin-injected group that received an AAV-NT-3 infection, a significant increase in NT-3 expression in the sciatic nerve was found compared to the PBS injected group (t = 5.282, df = 8, p<0.001).
source: However, in the lysolecithin-injected group that received an AAV-NT-3 infection, a significant increase in NT-3 expression in the sciatic nerve was found as compared to the PBS injected group (t = 5.282, df = 8, p<0.001, Figure 2—figure supplement 1K).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of immunofluorescence data measuring NT-3 expression in sciatic nerves.

claim: BMS locomotor test showed transient locomotor deficit at 1 day post lysolecithin injection (t = 3.841, df = 8, p<0.01), but was quickly returned to control levels at 7 and 14 days post-injection.
source: Notably, Basso Mouse Scale (BMS) locomotor test showed transient locomotor deficit at 1 day post lysolecithin injection (t = 3.841, df = 8, p<0.01), but was quickly returned to control levels at 7 and 14 days post-injection (7d: t = 2.86, df = 8, ns; 14d: t = 1.342, df = 8, ns; Figure 2—figure supplement 1L).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral assessment data showing recovery of locomotor function over time.

claim: Lysolecithin injection induced transient demyelination which effectively eliminated the infection barrier formed by the myelin sheath and facilitated AAV-NT-3 entry into the sciatic nerve axons.
source: These results collectively indicate that lysolecithin injection induced transient demyelination which effectively eliminated the infection barrier formed by the myelin sheath and facilitated AAV-NT-3 entry into the sciatic nerve axons.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple experimental results showing increased viral transduction after demyelination.

claim: The lysolecithin injection did not damage passing axons and no animals sustained any prolonged neurological deficits.
source: It is also important to note that the lysolecithin injection did not damage passing axons and no animals sustained any prolonged neurological deficits.
evidence: The claim is supported by axon density measurements and behavioral assessments showing no lasting damage.

claim: NT-3 immunofluorescent density revealed that the expression of NT-3 in the AAV-NT-3 injection group was significantly higher than that the AAV-GFP injection group (t = 6.695, df = 10, p<0.001).
source: NT-3 immunofluorescent density further revealed that the expression of NT-3 in the AAV-NT-3 injection group was significantly higher than that the AAV-GFP injection group (t = 6.695, df = 10, p<0.001, Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of immunofluorescence data measuring NT-3 expression in lumbar spinal cord.

claim: The concentration of NT-3 in the lumbar spinal cord after sciatic nerve infection of AAV-NT-3 showed an 8-fold increase in the amount of NT-3 compared to the AAV-GFP infection (t = 27.79, df = 4, p<0.001).
source: The concentration of NT-3 in the lumbar spinal cord after sciatic nerve infection of AAV-NT-3 showed an 8-fold increase in the amount of NT-3 as compared to the AAV-GFP infection (t = 27.79, df = 4, p<0.001, Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA assay data measuring NT-3 protein levels in lumbar spinal cord tissue.

claim: Biologically active NT-3 can be retrogradely transported to lumbar motoneurons, and can be expressed and released by transduced motoneurons in the lumbar spinal cord after their retrograde transport.
source: Thus, our data indicate that biologically active NT-3 can be retrogradely transported to lumbar motoneurons, and can be expressed and released by transduced motoneurons in the lumbar spinal cord after their retrograde transport.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple experimental results showing NT-3 expression in lumbar motoneurons after sciatic nerve injection.

claim: AAV-NT-3 treatment resulted in a significant and progressive recovery of locomotion compared to the AAV-GFP control group.
source: We found that AAV-NT-3 treatment resulted in a significant and progressive recovery of locomotion as compared to the AAV-GFP control group (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral assessment data showing improved BMS scores over time.

claim: The BMS scores at 4 and 5 weeks post-SCI in the AAV-NT-3 treated group were significantly higher than the AAV-GFP group (two-way ANOVA, time: F6, 162 = 245.2, p<0.001; column factor: F2, 27 = 298.3, p<0.001).
source: Repeated measures analysis of variance (ANOVA) revealed that the BMS scores at 4 and 5 weeks post-SCI in the AAV-NT-3 treated group were significantly higher than the AAV-GFP group (two-way ANOVA, time: F6, 162 = 245.2, p<0.001; column factor: F2, 27 = 298.3, p<0.001; Figure 4A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of repeated behavioral measurements using BMS scoring.

claim: Significant effect of AAV-NT-3 treatment was found on the rotarod run time at 5 weeks post-SCI compared to the control group receiving AAV-GFP (F2, 27 = 28.16, p<0.001).
source: Significant effect of AAV-NT-3 treatment was found on the rotarod run time at 5 weeks post-SCI as compared to the control group receiving AAV-GFP (F2, 27 = 28.16, p<0.001; Figure 4C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of rotarod performance test data.

claim: Administration of AAV-NT-3 significantly decreased footprint angle (F2, 27 = 9.19, p<0.001) at 5 weeks post-SCI.
source: TreadScan analysis (Figure 4E–H) demonstrated that administration of AAV-NT-3 significantly decreased footprint angle (F2, 27 = 9.19, p<0.001, Figure 4F) and improved footprint length (F2, 27 = 15.67, p<0.001, Figure 4G) and toe spread (F2, 27 = 9.45, p<0.001, Figure 4H) at 5 weeks post-SCI.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of gait analysis data from TreadScan.

claim: Administration of AAV-NT-3 significantly improved footprint length (F2, 27 = 15.67, p<0.001) at 5 weeks post-SCI.
source: TreadScan analysis (Figure 4E–H) demonstrated that administration of AAV-NT-3 significantly decreased footprint angle (F2, 27 = 9.19, p<0.001, Figure 4F) and improved footprint length (F2, 27 = 15.67, p<0.001, Figure 4G) and toe spread (F2, 27 = 9.45, p<0.001, Figure 4H) at 5 weeks post-SCI.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of gait analysis data from TreadScan.

claim: Administration of AAV-NT-3 significantly improved toe spread (F2, 27 = 9.45, p<0.001) at 5 weeks post-SCI.
source: TreadScan analysis (Figure 4E–H) demonstrated that administration of AAV-NT-3 significantly decreased footprint angle (F2, 27 = 9.19, p<0.001, Figure 4F) and improved footprint length (F2, 27 = 15.67, p<0.001, Figure 4G) and toe spread (F2, 27 = 9.45, p<0.001, Figure 4H) at 5 weeks post-SCI.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of gait analysis data from TreadScan.

claim: AAV-NT-3 treatment increased the number of early responses (ER) compared to the AAV-GFP control (χ2=0.833, p<0.001).
source: AAV-NT-3 treatment increased the number of ER as compared to the AAV-GFP control (χ2=0.833, p<0.001, Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of tcMMEP electrophysiological recordings.

claim: The AAV-NT-3 group demonstrated significantly increased amplitude in early and late responses compared to the AAV-GFP group after SCI (ER: F2, 15 = 15.67, p<0.001; LR: t = 7.630, df = 10, p<0.001).
source: However, compared to the AAV-GFP group, the AAV-NT-3 group demonstrated significantly increased amplitude (ER: F2, 15 = 15.67, p<0.001; LR: t = 7.630, df = 10, p<0.001, Figure 5G) and decreased latency (ER: F2, 15 = 16.55, p<0.001; LR: t = 3.993, df = 10, p<0.01, Figure 5H) in early and late responses as compared to the AAV-GFP group after SCI.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of tcMMEP amplitude measurements.

claim: The AAV-NT-3 group demonstrated significantly decreased latency in early and late responses compared to the AAV-GFP group after SCI (ER: F2, 15 = 16.55, p<0.001; LR: t = 3.993, df = 10, p<0.01).
source: However, compared to the AAV-GFP group, the AAV-NT-3 group demonstrated significantly increased amplitude (ER: F2, 15 = 15.67, p<0.001; LR: t = 7.630, df = 10, p<0.001, Figure 5G) and decreased latency (ER: F2, 15 = 16.55, p<0.001; LR: t = 3.993, df = 10, p<0.01, Figure 5H) in early and late responses as compared to the AAV-GFP group after SCI.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of tcMMEP latency measurements.

claim: Both behavioral and electrophysiological results indicate the positive influence of NT-3 on recovery of motor function after SCI.
source: Thus, both behavioral and electrophysiological results indicate the positive influence of NT-3 on recovery of motor function after SCI.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple behavioral and electrophysiological measurements showing improvements with NT-3 treatment.

claim: The number of MNs per animal labeled with BHRP did not differ across groups (F2, 21 = 0.517, ns).
source: The number of MNs per animal labeled with BHRP (F2, 21 = 0.517, ns, Figure 6—figure supplement 1C) or stained with Thionin (F2, 15 = 0.541, ns, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B) did not differ across groups (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of motoneuron counts showing no significant differences between groups.

claim: The number of MNs per animal stained with Thionin did not differ across groups (F2, 15 = 0.541, ns).
source: The number of MNs per animal labeled with BHRP (F2, 21 = 0.517, ns, Figure 6—figure supplement 1C) or stained with Thionin (F2, 15 = 0.541, ns, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B) did not differ across groups (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of motoneuron counts showing no significant differences between groups.

claim: The area of MN somata did not differ across treatment groups (F2, 21 = 1.647, ns).
source: The area of MN somata also did not differ across treatment groups (F2, 21 = 1.647, ns, Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of motoneuron somal area measurements.

claim: A thoracic contusive SCI did not cause lumbar MN loss.
source: These results indicate that a thoracic contusive SCI did not cause lumbar MN loss and that AAV-NT-3 infection did no affect MN somal size.
evidence: The claim is inferred from motoneuron count data showing no differences between sham and SCI groups.

claim: AAV-NT-3 infection did not affect MN somal size.
source: These results indicate that a thoracic contusive SCI did not cause lumbar MN loss and that AAV-NT-3 infection did no affect MN somal size.
evidence: The claim is inferred from motoneuron somal area measurements showing no differences between treatment groups.

claim: Following SCI, dendritic lengths of radial bins in the SCI + AAV GFP group reduced significantly.
source: Following SCI, dendritic lengths of these radial bins in the SCI + AAV GFP group reduced significantly.
evidence: The claim is supported by dendritic morphology measurements showing reduced dendritic length after SCI.

claim: Treatment with AAV-NT-3 attenuated SCI-induced reductions in dendritic length.
source: Treatment with AAV2-NT-3 attenuated these reductions.
evidence: The claim is supported by dendritic morphology measurements showing preserved dendritic length with NT-3 treatment.

claim: The dendritic length per TA motoneuron was significantly reduced in the AAV-GFP group and treatment with AAV-NT-3 significantly attenuated this dendritic atrophy.
source: The dendritic length per TA motoneuron was significantly reduced in the AAV-GFP group and treatment with AAV-NT-3 significantly attenuated this dendritic atrophy.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of dendritic length measurements.

claim: Following the T10 contusive SCI, the dendritic length per lumbar TA MNs was significantly decreased.
source: Following the T10 contusive SCI which did not affect lumbar MNs directly, the dendritic length per lumbar TA MNs was significantly decreased.
evidence: The claim is supported by dendritic morphology measurements showing reduced dendritic length after SCI.

claim: Treatment with AAV-NT-3 significantly attenuated SCI-induced MN dendritic atrophy (F2, 15 = 47.96, p<0.001).
source: However, treatment with AAV-NT-3 significantly attenuated SCI-induced MN dendritic atrophy (F2, 15 = 47.96, p<0.001, Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of dendritic length measurements comparing treatment groups.

claim: Treatment with AAV-NT-3 significantly attenuated SCI-induced reduction in MN dendritic length in specific radial bins (0 – 60 °, F2, 15 = 61.07, p<0.001; 60 – 120 °, F2, 15 = 11.59, p<0.001; 300 – 360 °, F2, 15 = 13.48, p<0.001).
source: Treatment with AAV-NT-3 significantly attenuated SCI-induced reduction in MN dendritic length in specific radial bins (0 – 60 °, F2, 15 = 61.07, p<0.001; 60 – 120 °, F2, 15 = 11.59, p<0.001; 300 – 360 °, F2, 15 = 13.48, p<0.001, Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of dendritic distribution measurements in specific spatial bins.

claim: There were strong correlations between the MN dendrite length per cell and both the BMS (r = 0.87, p<0.001) and rotarod (r = 0.71, p<0.001) behavioral assessments.
source: Notably, there were strong correlations between the MN dendrite length per cell and both the BMS (r = 0.87, p<0.001, Figure 6D) and rotarod (r = 0.71, p<0.001, Figure 6E) of behavioral assessments, indicating that motor functional improvements were likely influenced by increased MN dendritic arbors.
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis between morphological and behavioral measurements.

claim: Motor functional improvements were likely influenced by increased MN dendritic arbors.
source: Notably, there were strong correlations between the MN dendrite length per cell and both the BMS (r = 0.87, p<0.001, Figure 6D) and rotarod (r = 0.71, p<0.001, Figure 6E) of behavioral assessments, indicating that motor functional improvements were likely influenced by increased MN dendritic arbors.
evidence: The claim is inferred from correlation analysis showing relationship between dendritic morphology and functional outcomes.

claim: NT-3 has a wide range of effects on survival, biosynthetic activities and neuroprotective roles of dopaminergic neurons, likely via autocrine or paracrine mechanisms.
source: NT-3 has a wide range of effects on survival, biosynthetic activities and neuroprotective roles of dopaminergic neurons, likely via autocrine or paracrine mechanisms (Hyman et al., 1994; Seroogy et al., 1994).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies by Hyman et al., 1994 and Seroogy et al., 1994.

claim: A significant reduction of TH-IR dopaminergic axons innervating the lumbar ventral horn neuropil was found after a contusive SCI at T10.
source: We found a significant reduction of TH-IR dopaminergic axons innervating the lumbar ventral horn neuropil after a contusive SCI at T10 (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical data showing reduced TH-positive axon density after SCI.

claim: AAV-NT-3 infection resulted in a significant increase in the TH-IR axon density in the lumbar neuropil compared to the AAV-GFP (F2, 15 = 7.59, p<0.001).
source: Importantly, AAV-NT-3 infection resulted in a significant increase in the TH-IR axon density in the lumbar neuropil as compared to the AAV-GFP (F2, 15 = 7.59, p<0.001, Figure 7A and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of immunohistochemical data measuring TH-positive axon density.

claim: AAV-NT-3 treatment enhanced serotonergic descending innervation of lumbar MNs.
source: In this study, we found that AAV-NT-3 treatment enhanced serotonergic descending innervation of lumbar MNs which may form an anatomic basis for improved locomotor recovery.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical data showing increased 5-HT-positive axon density with NT-3 treatment.

claim: AAV-NT-3 treatment resulted in an about 1.5-fold increase in the 5-HT-IR axon density in the lumbar neuropil compared to the AAV-GFP control group (F2, 15 = 8.50, p<0.01).
source: Notably, AAV-NT-3 infection resulted in an about 1.5-fold increase in the 5-HT-IR axon density in the lumbar neuropil as compared to the AAV-GFP control group (F2, 15 = 8.50, p<0.01, Figure 7B and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of immunohistochemical data measuring 5-HT-positive axon density.

claim: AAV-NT-3 treatment significantly increased the density of dPST axons in the lumbar MN pool compared to the non-treated control group (F2, 15 = 8.89, p<0.01).
source: Consistent with 5-HT-IR and TH-IR axons, AAV-NT-3 treatment significantly increased the density of dPST axons in the lumbar MN pool as compared to the non-treated control group (F2, 15 = 8.89, p<0.01, Figure 7C and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of BDA-labeled axon density measurements.

claim: AAV-NT-3 treatment enhanced synaptic inputs of descending supraspinal (serotonergic, dopaminergic) and propriospinal (dPST) axons to lumbar MNs that remained intact but underwent atrophy and synaptic stripping after a thoracic contusive SCI.
source: These results collectively indicate that AAV-NT-3 treatment enhanced synaptic inputs of descending supraspinal (serotonergic, dopaminergic) and propriospinal (dPST) axons to lumbar MNs that remained intact but underwent atrophy and synaptic stripping after a thoracic contusive SCI.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple immunohistochemical measurements showing increased axon density with NT-3 treatment.

claim: The SYP density around ChAT-labeled MNs in the SCI + AAV-NT-3 group was significantly higher than that of the SCI + AAV GFP group (t = 2.63, p<0.05).
source: We found that the SYP density around ChAT-labeled MNs in the SCI + AAV-NT-3 group was significantly higher than that of the SCI + AAV GFP group (t = 2.63, p<0.05, Figure 8—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of synaptophysin immunofluorescence density measurements.

claim: AAV-NT-3 treatment prevented the decrease in SYP relative density (F2, 21 = 12.46, p<0.001).
source: AAV-NT-3 treatment prevented this decrease in SYP relative density (F2, 21 = 12.46, p<0.001, Figure 8A–B), increased the SYP density per MN soma per section (F2, 33 = 20.83, p<0.001, Figure 8C) as well as SYP density per dendritic segment per section (F2, 21 = 7.65, p<0.01, Figure 8D).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of synaptophysin density measurements around motoneurons.

claim: AAV-NT-3 treatment increased the SYP density per MN soma per section (F2, 33 = 20.83, p<0.001).
source: AAV-NT-3 treatment prevented this decrease in SYP relative density (F2, 21 = 12.46, p<0.001, Figure 8A–B), increased the SYP density per MN soma per section (F2, 33 = 20.83, p<0.001, Figure 8C) as well as SYP density per dendritic segment per section (F2, 21 = 7.65, p<0.01, Figure 8D).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of synaptophysin density measurements per motoneuron soma.

claim: AAV-NT-3 treatment increased SYP density per dendritic segment per section (F2, 21 = 7.65, p<0.01).
source: AAV-NT-3 treatment prevented this decrease in SYP relative density (F2, 21 = 12.46, p<0.001, Figure 8A–B), increased the SYP density per MN soma per section (F2, 33 = 20.83, p<0.001, Figure 8C) as well as SYP density per dendritic segment per section (F2, 21 = 7.65, p<0.01, Figure 8D).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of synaptophysin density measurements per dendritic segment.

claim: SCI induced reduction of synaptic contacts on motoneurons and their dendrites.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that SCI induced reduction of synaptic contacts on motoneurons and their dendrites, and that NT-3 overexpression by MNs and their dendrites may enhance the synaptic formation or attenuated the loss of synapses on MNs and their dendrites.
evidence: The claim is inferred from synaptophysin density measurements showing reduced synaptic markers after SCI.

claim: NT-3 overexpression by MNs and their dendrites may enhance the synaptic formation or attenuated the loss of synapses on MNs and their dendrites.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that SCI induced reduction of synaptic contacts on motoneurons and their dendrites, and that NT-3 overexpression by MNs and their dendrites may enhance the synaptic formation or attenuated the loss of synapses on MNs and their dendrites.
evidence: The claim is inferred from synaptophysin density measurements showing increased synaptic markers with NT-3 treatment.

claim: Following SCI in the AAV-GFP group, TA muscle weight decreased by 33.4% compared to the sham group.
source: Following SCI in the AAV-GFP group, TA muscle weight decreased by 33.4% as compared to the sham group, indicating that SCI induced TA muscle atrophy.
evidence: The claim is supported by muscle weight measurements showing reduced mass after SCI.

claim: The TA muscle weight in the AAV-NT-3 infected group increased 22.5% compared to the AAV-GFP treated group after SCI (F2, 15 = 29.96, p<0.001).
source: However, the TA muscle weight in the AAV-NT-3 infected group increased 22.5% as compared to the AAV-GFP treated group after SCI (F2, 15 = 29.96, p<0.001, Figure 9C).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of muscle weight measurements comparing treatment groups.

claim: TA muscle fiber diameter in the SCI + AAV GFP group was significantly reduced compared to the sham group.
source: TA muscle fiber diameter in the SCI + AAV GFP group was also significantly reduced as compared to the sham group (Figure 9A and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological measurements of muscle fiber diameter.

claim: AAV-NT-3 treatment significantly increased fiber diameter compared to the AAV-GFP group following SCI (F2, 15 = 35.15, p<0.001).
source: Notably, AAV-NT-3 treatment significantly increased fiber diameter as compared to the AAV-GFP group following SCI (F2, 15 = 35.15, p<0.001, Figure 9D).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of muscle fiber diameter measurements.

claim: Motor endplate densities were unaffected by the contusive SCI in different treatment groups (F2, 21 = 0.465, ns).
source: We also examined the density of motor endplates and found that they were unaffected by the contusive SCI in different treatment groups (F2, 21 = 0.465, ns, Figure 9B and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of motor endplate density measurements showing no significant differences.

claim: AAV-NT-3 infection significantly reduced TA muscle atrophy compared to the AAV-GFP following SCI, with increased TA muscle weights and fiber diameters compared to the untreated controls.
source: Collectively, these results indicate that AAV-NT-3 infection significantly reduced TA muscle atrophy as compared to the AAV-GFP following SCI, with increased TA muscle weights and fiber diameters compared to the untreated controls.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple muscle measurements showing protective effects of NT-3 treatment.

claim: AAV-NT-3 treatment had no effect on the percentages of lesion area (t = 0.689, df = 10, ns) at the lesion site compared to the AAV-GFP group.
source: Results showed that AAV-NT-3 treatment had no effect on the percentages of lesion area (t = 0.689, df = 10, ns, Figure 9—figure supplement 1A,C) and lesion volume (t = 0.073, df = 10, ns, Figure 9—figure supplement 1D) at the lesion site as compared to the AAV-GFP group.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of histological measurements showing no differences in lesion size.

claim: AAV-NT-3 treatment had no effect on lesion volume (t = 0.073, df = 10, ns) at the lesion site compared to the AAV-GFP group.
source: Results showed that AAV-NT-3 treatment had no effect on the percentages of lesion area (t = 0.689, df = 10, ns, Figure 9—figure supplement 1A,C) and lesion volume (t = 0.073, df = 10, ns, Figure 9—figure supplement 1D) at the lesion site as compared to the AAV-GFP group.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of histological measurements showing no differences in lesion volume.

claim: There was no difference in the percent of myelin sparing area between the AAV-NT-3 and AAV-GFP groups (t = 0.255, df = 10, ns).
source: Similarly, Luxol Fast Blue staining showed no difference in the percent of myelin sparing area between the two groups (t = 0.255, df = 10, ns, Figure 9—figure supplement 1B,E) indicating that local infection of lumbar MNs had no effect on the lesion size and myelin sparing rostral to the lumbar neuropil.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of myelin staining showing no differences between treatment groups.

claim: Local infection of lumbar MNs had no effect on the lesion size and myelin sparing rostral to the lumbar neuropil.
source: Similarly, Luxol Fast Blue staining showed no difference in the percent of myelin sparing area between the two groups (t = 0.255, df = 10, ns, Figure 9—figure supplement 1B,E) indicating that local infection of lumbar MNs had no effect on the lesion size and myelin sparing rostral to the lumbar neuropil.
evidence: The claim is inferred from histological measurements showing no differences in lesion characteristics at the injury site.

claim: Retrogradely transported AAV-NT-3 prevented dendrite atrophy, promoted descending serotonergic, dopaminergic and propriospinal axonal innervation and synaptic formation on lumbar MNs, attenuated muscle atrophy, and enhanced recovery of physiological and behavioral functions.
source: In conclusion, we have demonstrated that retrogradely transported AAV-NT-3 prevented dendrite atrophy, promoted descending serotonergic, dopaminergic and propriospinal axonal innervation and synaptic formation on lumbar MNs, attenuated muscle atrophy, and, consequently, enhanced recovery of physiological and behavioral functions.
evidence: The claim summarizes multiple experimental findings from the study.

claim: Retrograde transport of AAV-NT-3 may represent a promising therapeutic strategy for treating SCI.
source: These findings collectively suggest that retrograde transport of AAV-NT-3 may represent a promising therapeutic strategy for treating SCI.
evidence: The claim is a speculative conclusion based on the collective experimental findings.

claim: Circuitry within the lumbar spinal cord integrates afferent information from descending and segmental sources to coordinate the patterned firing of motor neuron pools.
source: Circuitry within the lumbar spinal cord integrates afferent information from descending and segmental sources to coordinate the patterned firing of motor neuron pools (Cazalets et al., 1995; Cazalets et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies by Cazalets et al., 1995 and 1996.

claim: Lumbar spinal MNs caudal to a thoracic contusive SCI underwent a marked reduction in their dendritic arbor.
source: We have previously reported that lumbar spinal MNs caudal to a thoracic contusive SCI underwent a marked reduction in their dendritic arbor (Byers et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2014a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies by the authors.

claim: Dendritic branching patterns and distribution determine important functional properties in MNs.
source: Dendritic branching patterns and distribution determine important functional properties in MNs (Cameron and Núñez-Abades, 2000), and thus preventing dendritic atrophy could be an important therapeutic target for restoring neural circuitry and functional recovery after SCI.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Cameron and Núñez-Abades, 2000.

claim: NT-3 is an attractive candidate for stimulating MN dendritic plasticity because it is a survival factor for MNs and is expressed by MNs.
source: Neurotrophin-3 (NT-3), a member of the neurotrophin family of proteins (Barbacid, 1994; Snider, 1994), is an attractive candidate for stimulating MN dendritic plasticity because it is a survival factor for MNs and is expressed by MNs, one of the main targets of descending axons of the spinal cord (Henderson et al., 1993; Buck et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple previous studies establishing NT-3's properties.

claim: Delivery of NT-3 via retrograde transport of AAV from triceps to cervical motoneurons led to reduced functional loss and anatomical reorganization of the CST following a dorsal lesion at C4-5.
source: In addition, a previous study has demonstrated that delivery of NT-3 via retrograde transport of AAV from triceps to cervical motoneurons led to reduced functional loss and anatomical reorganization of the CST following a dorsal lesion at C4-5 (Fortun et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Fortun et al., 2009.

claim: The AAV-mediated gene delivery has been reported as the most promising therapeutic transgene delivery system for prolonged, safe, and effective neurotrophin delivery.
source: The AAV-mediated gene delivery has been reported as the most promising therapeutic transgene delivery system for prolonged, safe, and effective neurotrophin delivery (Fortun et al., 2009; Petruska et al., 2010; Peng et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: NT-3 has an effect on dendrite morphogenesis in brain slice cultures and in proprioceptive axon patterning.
source: Earlier investigators showed an effect of NT-3 on dendrite morphogenesis in brain slice cultures and in proprioceptive axon patterning (Ernfors et al., 1994; McAllister et al., 1995; Patel et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Myelin provides a protective barrier to the nervous system that limits AAV viral infection.
source: We and others have reported that myelin provides a protective barrier to the nervous system that limits AAV viral infection (Zhou et al., 2003; Zhang et al., 2010; Hollis and Tuszynski, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: Lysolecithin-induced transient demyelination significantly increases the transduction efficiency of AAV.
source: Notably, lysolecithin-induced transient demyelination significantly increases the transduction efficiency of AAV.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the current study and previous literature.

claim: Direct injection of AAV-NT-3 into the lumbar MN region may cause direct damage and inflammation at the injection site.
source: Compared with direct injection of AAV-NT-3 into the lumbar MN region, which may cause direct damage and inflammation at the injection site, the sciatic nerve injection eliminates such damage and allows transducing a gene to specific populations of neurons.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from known effects of direct CNS injections.

claim: Caudal to an SCI, denervation of motoneurons (MNs) can result in dendritic reorganization or atrophy.
source: Caudal to an SCI, denervation of motoneurons (MNs) can result in dendritic reorganization or atrophy (Gazula et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Gazula et al., 2004.

claim: Descending spinal tracts are critically involved in specific functions, such as fine locomotor control, neuromodulation or initiation of rhythmic movements.
source: Descending spinal tracts are critically involved in specific functions, such as fine locomotor control, neuromodulation or initiation of rhythmic movements (Deumens et al., 2005; Jordan et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Contusive SCI can induce anatomically incomplete lesions whereas axons surrounding the lesion sites remain intact.
source: Contusive SCI can induce anatomically incomplete lesions whereas axons surrounding the lesion sites remain intact.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about contusive spinal cord injuries.

claim: Neurotrophic factors can support the sprouting of descending axons into injury-induced denervated areas to form new synapses.
source: Neurotrophic factors can support the sprouting of descending axons into injury-induced denervated areas to form new synapses (da Silva and Wang, 2011; Park and Poo, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The mesencephalic dopaminergic neurons represent a vital neuromodulatory component essential for vertebrate motor control.
source: The mesencephalic dopaminergic neurons represent a vital neuromodulatory component essential for vertebrate motor control (Ryczko et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Ryczko et al., 2016.

claim: Descending dopaminergic neurons are located in the A8, A9 and A10 groups of the mesencephalon and express the transmitter synthesizing enzyme tyrosine hydroxylase (TH).
source: Descending dopaminergic neurons are located in the A8, A9 and A10 groups of the mesencephalon and express the transmitter synthesizing enzyme tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) (Zaborszky and Vadasz, 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Zaborszky and Vadasz, 2001.

claim: In the spinal cord neuropil, TH-IR axons are of supraspinal origin and project to and beyond the lumbar spinal cord.
source: In the spinal cord neuropil, TH-IR axons are of supraspinal origin and project to and beyond the lumbar spinal cord.
evidence: The claim is based on established anatomical knowledge.

claim: The descending serotonergic pathway plays an important role in mediating descending influences on locomotion.
source: The descending serotonergic pathway plays an important role in mediating descending influences on locomotion (Bowker et al., 1983).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Bowker et al., 1983.

claim: Axons of the descending serotonergic pathway originate mainly from the nucleus raphe obscurus, the nucleus raphe pallidus, and the nucleus raphe magnus of the caudal brainstem, express the transmitter serotonin (5-HT), and project to and beyond the lumbar spinal cord.
source: Axons of this pathway originate mainly from the nucleus raphe obscurus, the nucleus raphe pallidus, and the nucleus raphe magnus of the caudal brainstem, express the transmitter serotonin (5-HT), and project to and beyond the lumbar spinal cord.
evidence: The claim is based on established anatomical knowledge.

claim: The descending propriospinal tract (dPST) axons play an essential role in mediating motor function.
source: The descending propriospinal tract (dPST) axons also play an essential role in mediating motor function.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about spinal cord anatomy and function.

claim: Following SCI, the dPST may serve as a functional relay conveying supraspinal motor command down to the distal spinal cord.
source: Following SCI, the dPST may serve as a functional relay conveying supraspinal motor command down to the distal spinal cord (Courtine et al., 2008; Deng et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Spared BDA-labeled dPST axons extended around the lesion through spared white matter.
source: We found that spared BDA-labeled dPST axons extended around the lesion through spared white matter (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by anterograde tracing data showing axon trajectories around the lesion.

claim: Motoneuron counts and somal size of TA MNs were not significantly affected by SCI.
source: Motoneuron counts and somal size of TA MNs were not significantly affected by SCI, confirming that TA motoneurons caudal to the injury site remain morphologically intact and are not directly traumatized by the injury.
evidence: The claim is supported by motoneuron count and size measurements showing no differences between sham and SCI groups.

claim: TA motoneurons caudal to the injury site remain morphologically intact and are not directly traumatized by the injury.
source: Motoneuron counts and somal size of TA MNs were not significantly affected by SCI, confirming that TA motoneurons caudal to the injury site remain morphologically intact and are not directly traumatized by the injury.
evidence: The claim is inferred from motoneuron count and size data showing no changes after SCI.

claim: Histological analysis showed no change in lesion area, volume, or myelin sparing in response to AAV-NT-3 treatment.
source: Moreover, histological analysis showed no change in lesion area, volume, or myelin sparing in response to AAV-NT-3 treatment.
evidence: The claim is supported by histological measurements at the lesion site.

claim: The T10 contusion level is rostral to the lumbar MNs and the retrogradely transported NT-3 did not reach the site of injury.
source: A possible explanation of the lack of histological changes at the lesion site is that the T10 contusion level is rostral to the lumbar MNs and the retrogradely transported NT-3 did not reach the site of injury.
evidence: The claim is a speculative explanation for the lack of lesion site changes.

claim: Contusive SCI results in the concomitant loss of descending pathways.
source: We have previously reported that contusive SCI results in the concomitant loss of descending pathways (Liu et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: Following SCI, CST axons fail to regenerate through and beyond the lesion site.
source: Following SCI, CST axons fail to regenerate through and beyond the lesion site (Sivasankaran et al., 2004; Liu et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The CST function could be mediated by its projection to other brainstem and spinal pathways that spared beyond the lesion site, which could provide a relay transmission for supraspinal motor commands.
source: The CST function, however, could be mediated by its projection to other brainstem and spinal pathways that spared beyond the lesion site, which could provide a relay transmission for supraspinal motor commands.
evidence: The claim is a speculative hypothesis about potential compensatory mechanisms.

claim: NT-3 is capable of promoting dPST axons to make new synaptic connections with lumbar MNs or ameliorate the SCI-induced loss of motor neuron inputs.
source: These data indicate that NT-3 is capable of promoting dPST axons to make new synaptic connections with lumbar MNs or ameliorate the SCI-induced loss of motor neuron inputs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from data showing increased dPST axon density with NT-3 treatment.

claim: Alterations of descending serotonergic and dopaminergic pathways have been correlated with sensory, motor, and autonomic disorders.
source: Alterations of descending serotonergic and dopaminergic pathways have been correlated with sensory, motor, and autonomic disorders (Hains et al., 2002; Lai et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: After SCI, most regenerating fibers have been shown to be serotonergic.
source: After SCI, most regenerating fibers have been shown to be serotonergic (Barritt et al., 2006; Alilain et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Serotonergic fibers have multiple functions in providing excitatory input to the ventral horn MNs and controlling the motor rhythm of hind limbs.
source: These fibers have multiple functions in providing excitatory input to the ventral horn MNs and controlling the motor rhythm of hind limbs (Barbeau and Rossignol, 1991; Alvarez et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Correlation between recovery of locomotor function after SCI and the presence of 5-HT-positive fibers caudal to the lesion has been described previously.
source: Correlation between recovery of locomotor function after SCI and the presence of 5-HT-positive fibers caudal to the lesion has been described previously (Erschbamer et al., 2007; Mountney et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Treatment with NT-3 resulted in dose-dependent increases in NT-3 expression in the number of TH-positive neurons, with similarly increased dopamine uptake activity and dopamine content.
source: A previous study demonstrated that NT-3 is localized to specific ventral mesencephalic regions containing dopaminergic cell bodies and that treatment with NT-3 resulted in dose-dependent increases in NT-3 expression in the number of TH-positive neurons, with similarly increased dopamine uptake activity and dopamine content (Hyman et al., 1994).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Hyman et al., 1994.

claim: Descending serotonergic, dopaminergic, and noradrenergic neurons express TrkB and TrkC.
source: It has been shown that descending serotonergic, dopaminergic, and noradrenergic neurons express TrkB and TrkC (King et al., 1999; Loudes et al., 1999) and can be stimulated to regenerate with NT-3 treatment following SCI (Bregman et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Descending neurons can be stimulated to regenerate with NT-3 treatment following SCI.
source: It has been shown that descending serotonergic, dopaminergic, and noradrenergic neurons express TrkB and TrkC (King et al., 1999; Loudes et al., 1999) and can be stimulated to regenerate with NT-3 treatment following SCI (Bregman et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Bregman et al., 1997.

claim: NT-3 displayed direct growth-stimulating and chemo-attractive effects on descending axons reaching the MNs after being retrogradely transported to the lumbar MNs.
source: It is possible that NT-3 displayed direct growth-stimulating and chemo-attractive effects on descending axons reaching the MNs after being retrogradely transported to the lumbar MNs.
evidence: The claim is a speculative hypothesis about the mechanism of NT-3 action.

claim: NT-3 has been shown to induce chemotropic regeneration of axons after SCI.
source: Indeed, NT-3 has been shown to induce chemotropic regeneration of axons after SCI (Alto et al., 2009; Hollis et al., 2010) and enhance axonal plasticity (Schnell et al., 1994).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: NT-3 has been shown to enhance axonal plasticity.
source: Indeed, NT-3 has been shown to induce chemotropic regeneration of axons after SCI (Alto et al., 2009; Hollis et al., 2010) and enhance axonal plasticity (Schnell et al., 1994).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Schnell et al., 1994.

claim: MNs and dendrites may locally secrete NT-3 to attract axons with the appropriate TrkC and/or p75 receptors.
source: Furthermore, MNs and dendrites may locally secrete NT-3 to attract axons with the appropriate TrkC and/or p75 receptors, as shown in MNs, propriospinal neurons and interneurons of various sizes (Merlio et al., 1992; Copray and Kernell, 2000; Gajewska-Woźniak et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is a speculative hypothesis supported by citations showing receptor expression.

claim: NT-3 could promote axon growth in multiple locomotor-related pathways including the CST, descending serotonergic and proprioceptive pathways.
source: Previous studies have shown that NT-3 could promote axon growth in multiple locomotor-related pathways including the CST, descending serotonergic and proprioceptive pathways (Grill et al., 1997; Zhou et al., 2003; Gajewska-Woźniak et al., 2013; Lai et al., 2013; Weishaupt et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: AAV-NT-3 induced the strengthening of connections of ventral MNs and establishing novel functional synaptic connections from descending axons to the dorsomedial interneurons after thoracic contusion.
source: One previous report demonstrated that AAV-NT-3 induced the strengthening of connections of ventral MNs and establishing novel functional synaptic connections from descending axons to the dorsomedial interneurons after thoracic contusion (Hunanyan et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Hunanyan et al., 2013.

claim: Overexpression of NT-3 on MNs enhances synaptic input on lumbar MNs, potentially contributing to improved functional outcomes.
source: In our case, we found that AAV-NT-3 increased synaptic-like contacts on lumbar MNs and dendrites, suggesting that overexpression of NT-3 on MNs enhances synaptic input on lumbar MNs, potentially contributing to improved functional outcomes.
evidence: The claim is inferred from synaptic density measurements and functional outcomes.

claim: The protection of muscle fibers could be a result of enhanced motoneuron activity, which could be caused by multiple actions of the NT-3 including the prevention of dendritic retraction, and enhanced neural circuitry on MNs.
source: The protection of muscle fibers could be a result of enhanced motoneuron activity, which could be caused by multiple actions of the NT-3 including the prevention of dendritic retraction, and enhanced neural circuitry on MNs.
evidence: The claim is a speculative hypothesis about the mechanism of muscle protection.

claim: NT-3 could be anterogradely transported to the terminals of MNs innervating the TA muscle to exert its protective effect directly on the muscle.
source: Alternatively, NT-3 could be anterogradely transported to the terminals of MNs innervating the TA muscle to exert its protective effect directly on the muscle.
evidence: The claim is a speculative alternative hypothesis about the mechanism of muscle protection.

claim: Preventing muscle atrophy is an important component to preserve functional limb use after SCI.
source: Preventing muscle atrophy is an important component to preserve functional limb use after SCI.
evidence: The claim is based on general knowledge about the importance of muscle preservation for function.

claim: This work is the first demonstration of NT-3 as an effective regulator of lumbar spinal circuit caudal to an SCI.
source: Thus, the work described herein is, to the best of our knowledge, the first demonstration of NT-3 as an effective regulator of lumbar spinal circuit caudal to an SCI, supporting a role for retrograde transport of NT-3 as a potential therapeutic strategy for SCI.
evidence: The claim is a statement about the novelty of the findings.

claim: Growing dendrites require anterograde NT-3 from their presynaptic partners during competitive dendrite growth.
source: A previous study reported that growing dendrites analogously require anterograde NT-3 from their presynaptic partners during competitive dendrite growth (Joo et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Joo et al., 2014.

claim: The mechanism of NT-3-mediated protection of motoneuron dendritic atrophy may involve NT-3's retrograde transport to and releasing from motoneurons.
source: The mechanism of NT-3-mediated protection of motoneuron dendritic atrophy may involve NT-3's retrograde transport to and releasing from motoneurons.
evidence: The claim is a speculative hypothesis about the mechanism of NT-3 action.

claim: Dendritic atrophy of MNs caudal to a SCI may reflect deafferentation resulting from the loss of descending motor and propriospinal tracts.
source: Therefore, the dendritic atrophy of MNs caudal to a SCI we observed may reflect deafferentation resulting from the loss of descending motor and propriospinal tracts.
evidence: The claim is a speculative interpretation of the observed dendritic atrophy.

claim: Dendritic atrophy is an important contributor to movement deficits.
source: A significant finding of this study is that the dendritic atrophy correlates well with behavioral deficits, suggesting that dendritic atrophy is an important contributor to movement deficits.
evidence: The claim is inferred from correlation analysis between dendritic morphology and behavioral outcomes.

claim: Spinal cord neurons caudal to the lesion responded to injury with marked dendritic retraction.
source: After SCI, surviving MNs caudal to the lesion responded to injury with marked dendritic retraction (Byers et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Byers et al., 2012.

claim: Dendritic morphology is a critical determinant of neuronal function.
source: Changes in dendritic morphological patterns have drawn a lot of interest, particularly because dendritic morphology is a critical determinant of neuronal function.
evidence: The claim is based on established neuroscience knowledge.

claim: Spinal MNs caudal to the lesion site underwent marked reduction in their dendritic arbor, especially in the dorsomedial portion of the ventral horn where both reticulospinal and propriospinal projections terminate.
source: We confirmed that spinal MNs caudal to the lesion site underwent marked reduction in their dendritic arbor, especially in the dorsomedial portion of the ventral horn where both reticulospinal and propriospinal projections terminate (Jones and Yang, 1985; Martin et al., 1985), and disruption of which resulted in hindlimb motor deficits (Loy et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and citations to previous anatomical studies.

claim: Disruption of reticulospinal and propriospinal projections resulted in hindlimb motor deficits.
source: We confirmed that spinal MNs caudal to the lesion site underwent marked reduction in their dendritic arbor, especially in the dorsomedial portion of the ventral horn where both reticulospinal and propriospinal projections terminate (Jones and Yang, 1985; Martin et al., 1985), and disruption of which resulted in hindlimb motor deficits (Loy et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Loy et al., 2002.
